title: TB9-31362
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) which found that they are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant/ PA) and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellant) are citizens of Colombia. They are appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) which found that they are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.

The PA alleges that she was first threatened by the Clan Del Golfo (CDG) in January 2016 who wanted her assistance in laundering money through her employment. She received threatening calls again in February and March of 2016. The Appellant alleges that she sought assistance from the authorities, but no help was forthcoming. The Appellant further alleges that she moved to live with her sister in XXXX 2016 because of these threats. She was threatened again by phone in November 2016 and again in June 2017.

The Appellants left Colombia in XXXX 2017 to visit the PA's boyfriend in the U.S., and the PA and her boyfriend got married the same month. However, after being married the PA's partner became abusive and controlling. The Appellants left the U.S. for Canada in XXXX 2018 and made their claims for refugee protection the next day. The PA alleges that she is still at risk in Colombia from the CDG who are seeking to retaliate against her for failing to comply with their demands, and also by her abusive ex-spouse in the U.S., whom the PA alleges is trying to locate her since she left him.
The RPD found that the PA was not credible because of several inconsistencies, omissions, and implausibilities with her evidence, as well as credibility problems with her sister's witness evidence.

The Appellants argue that the RPD made several errors in reaching its credibility findings, including examining the PA's evidence microscopically and failing to consider and apply the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines.1 The Appellants also allege that the RPD erred in failing to consider the PA's corroborating documentary evidence.

The Appellants are seeking an appeal hearing. However, given that the Appellants have not provided any new evidence on appeal, I do not have jurisdiction to hold a hearing pursuant to subsection 110(6) of IRPA, and must proceed without a hearing on the basis of the record of proceedings of the RPD. As such, the Appellant's hearing request is denied.
I find that the determinative issue in this case is credibility, and that the Appellants have failed to prove the credibility of their allegations on a balance of probabilities.

My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.2 Although I do not agree with all of the RPD's credibility findings, I find that there are sufficient credibility concerns in this instance to find that the Appellants have not proven their allegations on a balance of probabilities. Inconsistency about when the Appellant was threatened with death

I find that a negative credibility inference reasonably flows from the inconsistency in the PA's evidence as to when she was threatened with death by the CDG. While the Appellant testified that she was threatened in the January 2016 call with death if she reported the call to her employer, her BOC narrative only stated that she was told "there would be consequences" if she did not comply with their demands in this first call. Furthermore, I note that the Appellant's BOC as related to this phone call notes that "[she] did not take the interaction seriously" and that "she suspected this was an empty threat and moved on". Rather, the Appellant's BOC notes that she was threatened with death in the second call, which occurred a month later. I find that there is an inconsistency between the Appellant's BOC and her testimony about when she was threatened with death by the CDG and how seriously she took this threat. The Appellant argues that whether there was an implicit or explicit death threat during the first phone call she received is a minor issue and does not warrant a negative credibility finding.3 I do not agree. Rather, I find that when the Appellant was threatened with death is significant and relates directly to not only the death threat she faced, but also how seriously she took the first threatening call. Furthermore, I do not accept the Appellant's submission that the Gender Guidelines explain this inconsistency between the Appellant's written evidence and oral testimony.4 Rather, I find that, if these calls had occurred as alleged, the Appellant would have been able to provide consistent evidence about what occurred in these calls, when she threatened with death, and how this threat then affected her actions thereafter. Why she did not report threats to her employer

When asked by the RPD, the Appellant acknowledged that there are corporate policies requiring that incidents such as these threatening calls be reported to the company. However, the Appellant testified that the threat to her life contained in the first phone call was the reason she did not report this call to her superiors, as she felt that someone in the company was spying on her on behalf of the CDG. However, this does not align with the Appellant's BOC narrative, noted above, in which she testified, about the January call, that "[she] did not take the interaction seriously" and that "she suspected this was an empty threat and moved on." As noted by the RPD, the Appellant stated in her BOC that she gave little concern to the first phone call, but in her testimony she then attempted to rationalize her failure to follow corporate reporting policies by saying she was fearful of the first call because of a death threat. I do not find that this is a minor inconsistency, nor that the RPD was microscopic in its examination of this evidence as alleged by the Appellant. Rather, I find that a negative credibility inference follows from the additional inconsistency between the Appellant's BOC narrative that she was not fearful after the first phone call and her testimony that her fear after the first call was what prevented her from reporting this incident to her employers. Furthermore, I note the Appellant's BOC narrative does not mention that she was concerned about someone at work spying on her until November 2016, months after the Appellant testified in the RPD hearing that this concern affected her decision not to report the early 2016 phone calls to her superiors. Failure to demonstrate she took serious steps to change jobs

I also find that a negative credibility inference reasonably flows from the Appellant's failure to demonstrate that she took serious steps to change her job after these threats began. Indeed, the Appellant stated that she moved in with her sister in XXXX 2016 because of these threats. However, she did not provide credible evidence that she made any serious efforts to obtain other employment, either within her company or elsewhere. Indeed, I do not find that the Appellant would reasonably continue in the same employment for 16 months at the same location at which she became a target of the CDG if she had been threatened by them as alleged without making serious efforts to change jobs. Furthermore, I do not find that the Appellant's explanation that she was concerned that she would be unable to find another job that paid as much and she needed to support her parents is a convincing reason not to make serious efforts to find new employment where she alleges having been at risk at her current employment by the CDG. Delay in telling her sister about threats and when her family was threatened

Another credibility concern regarding the Appellant's testimony and allegations flows from the Appellant's delay in telling her sister about the CDG's threats as well as the PA's inconsistent evidence regarding why she did not tell her sister about these threats sooner. Indeed, the Appellant's BOC states that she told her sister about the CDG threats in January 2018, when the Appellant was in her last two weeks in the USA. When asked why she did not tell her sister about these threats sooner, the Appellant testified that CDG had warned her not to say anything to her family members. However, according to the PA's BOC narrative, she was not warned about telling her family about the threats until the third threatening phone call she received in November 2016, which was long after the Appellant had moved in with her sister as a result of these threats in XXXX 2016. When asked, the Appellant said that the CDG had "always told her that" and that the fact that this information was missing from her BOC as a part of the content of the earlier calls was an omission or mistake.

I do not accept the Appellant's explanation as reasonable in this instance, and do not find it credible that she would move in with her sister in XXXX 2016 to avoid these threats and stay with her for almost a year and a half - thereby exposing her sister to risk - without telling her about the alleged threats against them. This is especially so when the PA alleges that the CDG named her sister specifically in its June 2017 call and stated that they knew where her sister worked. Despite this personal threat against her sister, however, the PA alleges that she did not tell her sister anything about the threats for six months after leaving Colombia. I find that a negative credibility inference flows from the Appellant's failure to tell her sister about the threats against them until 2018, that being months after she had left Colombia, and also for the inconsistent evidence she provided about when the CDG threatened her family, be it initially in the first call in January 2016 as she testified, or not until the November 2016 call as per her BOC. Inconsistencies and omissions in sister's witness evidence

In this instance, a negative credibility inference also flows from the Appellant's sister's testimony in support of the Appellant's claim given a major inconsistency within her sister's evidence. When asked when the Appellant stayed with her, her sister first stated that she stayed with her from 2014-2015. She then stated it was 2016. When asked to clarify this testimony, she stated that her sister stayed with her from XXXX 2016 to XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, that being for a duration of 5 months. She then stated the correct year was 2017. However, the BOC narratives for both the witness and the Appellant notes that the Appellant stayed with her sister for 17 months, between 2016 and 2017. By way of explanation for this inconsistency, the witness stated that she was confused. However, I find that this is a major inconsistency about a significant part of the Appellant's claim, that being how long she stayed with her sister after receiving threats from the CDG before fleeing Colombia. I find that the witness's evidence in this case lacked credibility about how long the Appellant stayed with her, and significantly undermines the credibility of the PA's allegations that she moved in with her sister to hide and for safety reasons.

The Appellant's sister's testimony also included significant omissions regarding the details of the threats she received from the CDG as compared to her BOC narrative, including that the person who threatened her said he was part of the CDG, and also that he made specific and detailed threats against the witness's family members, including her daughter. When asked about this omission, the witness stated that there were so many events and that she had filed a report. I do not find that this reasonably explains the significant omissions in her oral testimony about the threats facing both the witness and her family - including her daughter. Rather, I find that the witness's credibility and the credibility of the PA's allegations is negatively affected by these omissions. Credibility Conclusion

Sworn evidence is presumed to be true unless there is a valid reason to doubt its truthfulness.5 Reasons to doubt the credibility of sworn evidence include inconsistencies and omissions in the Appellant's evidence. Furthermore, even if they may be insufficient when considered in isolation, the accumulation of contradictions, inconsistencies, and omissions regarding crucial elements of a refugee claim can support a negative conclusion about an applicant's credibility.6 I find that this is an instance where an accumulation of inconsistencies and omissions in the PA's and the witness's evidence about the alleged events means that the Appellant has failed to prove the credibility of her allegations.

While the RPD found several more areas of the Appellant's evidence to lack credibility - for instance, the Appellant's failure to claim asylum in the U.S., the Appellant's failure to update her BOC to reflect her sister's arrival in Canada, and the Appellant's failure to present her second witness for questioning, among others - I do not find that these other findings are sufficient to sustain a negative credibility finding. Nevertheless, I find that the numerous and significant credibility issues noted above are sufficient to uphold the RPD's finding that the Appellant has not proven, on a balance of probabilities, that she was threatened by the CDG as alleged, such that she would face a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a s. 97 risk upon her return to Colombia.

I am also mindful of the Appellant's argument that the RPD erred in failing to conduct and independent analysis of the documentary evidence before it, and that a negative finding of some of the Appellant's testimony does not relieve the RPD from making a determination on the totality of the evidence.7 However, I agree with the RPD that case law suggests that a finding of a general lack of credibility can extend to supporting evidence. Indeed, as noted by the Federal Court in Gebetas, a finding of a lack of credibility can affect all relevant evidence submitted by an applicant, including documentary evidence, and ultimately cause the rejection of a claim.8 The Federal Court of Appeal has found similarly, noting in Sheikh, that: Even without disbelieving every word [a claimant] has uttered, a ... panel may reasonably find him so lacking in credibility that it concludes that there is no credible evidence relevant to his claim ... In other words, a general finding of a lack of credibility on the part of the applicant may conceivably extend to all relevant information emanating from his testimony.9

I find that the Appellant's corroborating evidence in this instance (including, for instance, denunciations made to authorities by the Appellant and her sister) are owed little weight in this case because of the significant credibility concerns noted above regarding the PA's allegations. Rather, based on these credibility concerns, I do not find that that the Appellant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that these documents are based on genuine events as alleged. Moreover, I do not find that this evidence provides persuasive corroboration of the alleged risk facing the Appellant in light of these credibility concerns or is sufficient, in and of itself, to prove the Appellant's allegations on a balance of probabilities in light of the multiple credibility issues with the Appellant's and her witness's evidence.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
